_meta.note: AI roster scouting reports keyed by team (players.team value). Generated by roster_reports.workflow.js from build_roster_inputs.py output. Sample seeded manually; run the workflow to fill the rest.

bench.helps: This is where the real depth and shooting live. Kolby King (Utah State, 39.3% 3P, 47.7% FG, elite 0.8 TO) is a plug-and-play low-mistake combo guard; Adam Olsen (South Alabama, 16.7 ppg, 39.5% 3P) is a bench bucket who genuinely spaces the floor; and Owen Freeman (Creighton, 60.2% FG, 0.8 blk) plus 7-1 Bukky Oboye (66.7% FG, 1.2 blk, Santa Clara) give you two more efficient, shot-blocking bigs. That's a five-deep frontcourt rotation and two shooters — a bench that's arguably better-spaced than the starters.
bench.hurts: The problem is usage, not talent. Olsen was a 35.8-mpg No. 1 option who now has to accept a bench scoring role — that's a hard adjustment for a 16.7 ppg guy. And past the top nine it falls off a cliff: Walker (68) and Williams (72) are projects, and Walker's shooting line (52.9% 3P) comes on 5 mpg — statistical noise, not a rotation shooter. Foul trouble or an injury to a big thins this out fast.

coach.might: Start the authored five — Pettiford and Kimble in the backcourt, Overton on the wing, Dowd and freshman Ngoy up front — lean on guard ball-pressure and offensive-glass size, and ride Olsen as the instant-offense sixth man while Freeman and Oboye rotate at the five.
should: Weaponize Pettiford as a driver, not a shooter — put him in ball-screens with Overton and Dowd as the release valves so his 29% from three never has to matter; let him attack the rim and kick, and hide the non-shooting by surrounding him with your 39%+ guys.

Stagger Pettiford and Kimble so one lead guard is always on the floor — playing them together invites a usage collision and leaves the second unit without a creator; bring Kimble back with the King/Olsen group so the bench has real shot-making.

Give Olsen starter-level minutes even off the bench — a 16.7-ppg, 39.5% shooter is your best floor-spacer AND a bigger wing than Overton; closing lineups of Kimble–Overton–Olsen–Dowd–big is your most spaced five and should finish tight games.

Have a proven-big contingency ready behind Ngoy — if the freshman five gets into foul trouble or gets bullied by SEC size, Freeman (60.2% FG) and 7-1 Oboye (1.2 blk) are the safety net; don't let the projection-over-production bet cost you March games.

Auburn.essence: Auburn is a top-heavy, guard-driven SEC roster built around a genuine returning star in Tahaad Pettiford (86) and a rebuilt supporting cast — five of the top nine came through the portal. The identity is downhill guard pressure and interior size, NOT clean spacing: for all the scoring, only Kevin Overton (41.3%) truly stretches the floor in the starting five, and Pettiford's 29% from three on real volume is a spacing leak the whole offense has to work around. The strength is a deep, physical, shot-blocking frontcourt (Dowd, Ngoy, Freeman, Oboye) and multiple 15+ ppg creators; the tension is usage — Pettiford, Kimble, and sixth-man Olsen were all "the guy" somewhere, and someone has to give up shots.

second_unit.strength: A bench-heavy lineup of King–Olsen–Freeman/Oboye is actually better-spaced than the starters: King (39.3%) and Olsen (39.5%) are both above the 39% bar, and the second-unit bigs finish at 60%+ (Freeman 60.2%, Oboye 66.7%). You can bring pace and efficiency without a scoring drop-off — the grade cliff from starters (80-86) to the top bench (77-79) is barely two points.
second_unit.weakness: There's no true point guard organizing it — King is a 1.6-apg scorer, not a distributor, so when Pettiford and Kimble both sit, playmaking and shot creation dry up. And every second-unit big is a finisher, not a floor-spacer at the five, so late-clock half-court possessions can stall into contested twos.

flaws.b: Pettiford at 29% from three on starter minutes (39.3% FG) lets defenses go under every screen and sag off in the half court. Your primary initiator being a non-shooter collapses the spacing that Overton and Dowd's gravity create.
flaws.t: The point guard can't shoot it

flaws.b: Overton (41.3%) is it. Kimble (34.8%) is streaky, Pettiford (29%) is a negative, Dowd (33.3%) is a bonus at best, and Ngoy is an unproven freshman. Defenses can load the strong side and dare four of five to beat them from deep.
flaws.t: Only one reliable shooter in the first five

flaws.b: Kimble was the featured scorer at EKU (18.0 ppg); Pettiford is the returning star who needs touches. Both are score-first lead guards with 2.2 and 2.6 TO — neither has played extended minutes as a spot-up secondary, and their assist rates (3.8, 3.2) aren't high enough to guarantee the other stays fed.
flaws.t: Two alpha guards, one ball

flaws.b: Ngoy has null stats — no proven rebounding, foul-rate, or rim-protection numbers against grown SEC bigs. Starting an 85-graded projection at center in the toughest league in the country is a bet, not a known quantity.
flaws.t: A freshman five with zero college sample

positives.b: Thomas Dowd (Troy) put up 10.1 rpg and 1.3 blk in 36 mpg at 44.1% — a two-way PF who cleans the glass and defends without needing the ball (2.1 apg, just 1.4 TO). He's the connective tissue this starting five needs.

Pettiford (15.4/3.8 apg, 82.5% FT, 1.1 stl) and Kimble (18.0/2.6 stl, 85.1% FT) are a downhill, ball-pressuring backcourt that gets to the line and forces turnovers. Kimble's 2.6 steals is a legitimate defensive weapon at the point of attack.

Kevin Overton is the cleanest offensive fit on the roster — 41.3% from three, 44.6% FG, 86% FT, and only 1.0 TO per game on 14.1 ppg. He's the low-usage, high-efficiency wing every ball-dominant guard duo wants next to them.

Narcisse Ngoy is a 6-10 freshman graded 85 — the highest-rated non-Pettiford player on the roster. If he's ready, the starting front line is 6-8/6-10 with rim protection; that ceiling is why the coach authored him into the five over proven vets.

bench.helps: Genuinely deep on the wing with shooting. Tyler Betsey (78, 40.7% from three at Cincinnati) and Dawson Baker (75, 47.4% from three, 88.9% FT) are two more floor-spacers who keep the spacing intact when Wright sits, and Nate Pickens (69) is a 9.8-ppg, 39.2% combo guard who can run second units. The starter-to-bench grade drop-off is gentle on the perimeter — this is a real nine-deep shooting rotation.
bench.hurts: The depth is all guard/wing; the frontcourt cupboard is bare. Behind Whalin and Urbaniak, the only bigs are Khadim Mboup (73 — 2.2 ppg, a 23.1% FT non-shooter defenses ignore) and Adam Stewart (59, 1 career minute). If Wright or Chandler misses time the perimeter absorbs it; if a big gets in foul trouble against Big-12 size, there is no answer.

coach.might: Play through Wright in ball screens with four shooters around him, start the two projection freshmen (Branch, Urbaniak) on grade, and lean on the deep wing rotation to keep fresh shooters on the floor — riding elite spacing and a clean usage hierarchy.
should: Solve the rim, or scheme around it. With no shot-blocker, commit to a disciplined drop-or-pack scheme that walls off the paint and dares Big-12 teams to beat you from three — you have the personnel to switch 1 through 3, so switch everything on the perimeter and gang-rebound to cover the size deficit.

Don't hand the freshmen the keys on faith. Branch (83) and Urbaniak (75) are unproven; script their minutes and have a proven fallback — slide Betsey into the wing start and lean on Mboup's 5.1-rpg rebounding when the freshmen struggle, rather than riding grades into a January loss.

Weaponize the spacing with Wright in the two-man game. Five 39%+ shooters means every Wright ball screen is a 4-out advantage; make the rim-runner and short-roll reads the offense's spine so his 4.6 assists climb and the non-creators just knock down catch-and-shoot looks.

Hide the non-spacers. Mboup (23.1% FT, 16.7% 3P) and Whalin (68.8% FT) can't be left on the floor together in crunch time — go small with Whalin as the lone big surrounded by shooters late, and keep Mboup's minutes to defense-and-rebound bursts against opponents you can't otherwise match up with.

BYU.essence: A returning-star build, not a teardown: Robert Wright (92, 18.1/4.6/41% from three) is the unquestioned engine, and Kevin Young has surrounded him with a portal-and-freshman supporting cast that shoots it at a high level but is dangerously light in the middle. Five projected 39%+ shooters give this team genuine spacing and a clean usage hierarchy — one alpha, everyone else complementary — which is the opposite of most portal rosters' ball-dominance logjam. The catch is size and rim protection: nobody on the roster blocked even half a shot per game, there is no proven center, and two of the five starters (Branch, Urbaniak) are unproven freshmen carrying projection-inflated grades. Elite guard play and floor spacing, with a soft interior and a lot of faith placed in players who haven't done it yet.

second_unit.strength: Bench-heavy spacing and shot-making: a Pickens–Baker–Betsey wing group can put four 39%+ shooters on the floor at once, keeping the offense humming and the driving lanes open even with Wright resting. Baker's 47.4%/88.9% splits make him a lethal off-ball connector.
second_unit.weakness: No size, no rim protection, no interior rebounding, and no secondary creator. Mboup can't be guarded on offense (23.1% FT, 16.7% from three), Stewart is untested, and without Wright there's no one to consistently generate a good shot off the dribble. The second unit is a shooting group that gets hunted inside and can go cold with no bailout.

flaws.b: Blocks across the roster are near-zero: Whalin 0.3, Chandler 0.3, Urbaniak unproven, and the only listed center (Adam Stewart, 6-11) played 1 minute at TCU. Wright is 6-1, Chandler 6-5, Branch a freshman wing. Big-12 bigs will get to the rim and there is no eraser behind the defense.
flaws.t: Nobody protects the rim

flaws.b: Branch (83) and Urbaniak (75) are graded on projection with zero college sample. That's a lot of season-opening trust for a Big-12 contender: a 6-7 freshman wing at the 3 and a 6-9 international freshman as a starting big. If either isn't ready, the margin thins fast.
flaws.t: Two unproven freshmen in the starting five

flaws.b: No starter rebounds at a high rate — Wright's 3.5 is guard-good, Whalin 3.9 in 20.5 min is ordinary for a 6-10 four, and Mboup's 5.1 in 15.6 comes off the bench. Playing Wright/Chandler/Branch across three spots means giving up size at the wing and getting pounded on the offensive glass.
flaws.t: Undersized and mediocre on the glass

flaws.b: At 34% from three and 68.8% FT, Jake Whalin is the one starter defenses can help off. As a 6-10 four who scored 5.3 a game at Clemson, he neither stretches the floor cleanly nor protects the rim — a functional role player, not a plus-starter (76).
flaws.t: Whalin is the shaky spacing link

positives.b: Robert Wright (92) is unambiguously the guy — 18.1 ppg, 4.6 apg, 41% from three, 82.1% FT, 2.2 TO on 34.8 min. No usage collision behind him: Chandler was a 9.7-ppg role player at Kentucky, Whalin a 5.3-ppg energy big at Clemson. Everyone else accepts a secondary role, which is exactly what you want around a lead guard this good.

Wright 41%, Chandler 41% (6-5 wing), plus Betsey 40.7% and Baker 47.4% off the bench. You cannot sag off this perimeter, and that opens driving lanes for Wright. Chandler at 6-5, 43.5% FG, 83.3% FT is a legitimate 3-and-D complement who takes care of the ball (1.1 TO).
Wright's 4.6-to-2.2 assist-to-turnover as a high-usage lead guard is excellent; Chandler's 1.1 TO in 27 minutes is elite ball security. This starting group won't beat itself with live-ball giveaways.

bench.helps: This is the roster's quiet strength. Christian Hammond carries an 85 grade — higher than any starter but Lubin — and scored 15.6 on 39.3% from three with 1.2 steals at Santa Clara. That's a starter-quality lead guard coming off the bench: he can close games, shoulder the scoring when Edmead rests, and brings the on-ball defense the starting group lacks. Darius Adams (80) is a third ball-handler, and Jurkovic (79) plus Wilkins add frontcourt bodies. The top of this bench barely drops off from the first five.
bench.hurts: Below Hammond and Adams it thins fast and the fit gets awkward. Adams shot 24.8% from three and 35.4% from the field — a volume guard who was not efficient. Emuobor (10.7% from three), Keene (2.6 ppg despite 22 minutes at Boise State), Brim (6.2 mpg) and Hall (65 grade, JUCO) are role-limited or unproven. Jurkovic, Wilkins and Whitty have no college sample at all — those grades are projection, not production.

coach.might: Run the obvious lineup — Edmead on the ball, McNeil and Yalaho spacing the wings, Lubin and Evans anchoring the paint — and bring Hammond as an instant-offense sixth man, leaning on size, rebounding and Evans' rim protection to grind games out in the half court.
should: Stagger Edmead and Hammond so one 84/85-grade lead guard is always on the floor, and never let the offense run through Adams as the primary creator — his 24.8%/35.4% line will stall possessions when the real ball-handlers rest.

Close tight games with Hammond BESIDE Edmead, not instead of him: two guards who both shoot ~39% is your best five-out look. McNeil is the third spacer, Evans stays as the rim protector, and you sit the second non-shooting big.

Weaponize Yalaho as a pick-and-pop four and run Edmead–Yalaho ball screens to drag the opponent's rim protector out to the arc — that action is what makes the Lubin/Evans non-shooting minutes survivable.
Manage the non-shooters by lineup, not by hope: never play Adams and Emuobor together, and never stack Lubin and Evans without both Yalaho and McNeil on the floor, or the paint gets walled off.

NC-State.essence: A heavy portal rebuild with an unusually clear identity. Justin Gainey remade this roster through the transfer market — 10 transfers plus two freshmen around just two returners (Paul McNeil and Ven-Allen Lubin) — but this isn't a chaotic collection of names. It's a genuine size-and-rim-protection team: a 6-8/6-9/6-10 frontcourt that rebounds (three starters at 5.7+ boards) and erases shots (Kyle Evans at 3.3 blocks), a clear lead guard in Preston Edmead, real wing spacing from McNeil (42.7%) and stretch-four Eemeli Yalaho (39.8%), and — the hidden edge — a starter-quality lead guard, Christian Hammond (85 grade), coming off the bench. The questions are just as clear: only one true playmaker on the floor at a time, two non-shooting bigs who can tighten the paint, and a second unit whose spacing collapses the moment Hammond sits.

second_unit.strength: Hammond is a genuine sixth-man bucket-getter and the best perimeter defender on the roster (1.2 steals) — a bench unit you can actually win minutes with, not merely survive. When he's on the floor the second unit has a lead guard who was 'the guy' at his last stop.
second_unit.weakness: Spacing craters the moment Hammond has non-shooters around him. Adams (24.8% from three, 35.4% from the field) and Emuobor (10.7% from three) are two players defenses will flat-out ignore; put them on the floor together and the driving lanes Hammond needs disappear. The reserve wings offer defense and rebounding but no shooting to punish a sagging defense.

flaws.b: Edmead's 4.4 assists are the only real playmaking in the starting five — McNeil 0.8, Lubin 0.9, Evans 0.9. Pressure him or sit him and the offense has no secondary engine on the floor. Everything runs through one 6-1 guard.
flaws.t: One creator, and then nothing

flaws.b: Lubin (27.3% from three) and Evans (20% on almost nothing) hand a chunk of that spacing back. Against a switchy, paint-walling defense the floor tightens fast, and the offense leans hard on Yalaho and McNeil being the only release valves.
flaws.t: Two non-shooters up front

flaws.b: Edmead managed 0.5 steals and McNeil 0.6 — this group protects the rim but generates almost zero havoc on the ball. The roster's best perimeter defender, Hammond (1.2 steals), is sitting on the bench when the game tips.
flaws.t: No ball pressure from the starting guards

flaws.b: 2.2 TOs is a real number when there is no backup creator beside him. Live-ball giveaways turn into transition points against a team that isn't built to get back and run.
flaws.t: Edmead's turnovers as the lone initiator

positives.b: Kyle Evans blocked 3.3 per game at UC Irvine while shooting 62% — a legitimate 6-10 back-line eraser. Lubin adds 0.9 behind him. Opponents do not get clean looks at the basket, and that's a foundation you can win ugly with.
positives.t: Rim protection to build a defense around

positives.b: Yalaho is a 6-8 stretch four who hit 39.8% from three, and McNeil is an elite movement shooter at 42.7% on the wing. That pairing is what lets the two non-shooting bigs (Lubin, Evans) operate — the defense can't pack the paint without leaving a 40% shooter.
positives.t: The frontcourt actually spaces the floor

positives.b: McNeil (13.8 on 42.7%, a microscopic 0.4 TOs) and Lubin (13.6 on 66.8% from the field) put up points without plays being called for them. They punish help defense rather than demand touches — the perfect fit next to a ball-dominant guard.
Evans 8.7, Lubin 7.1, Yalaho 5.7 — three frontcourt rebounders who each cleared 5.7. Defensive-board control and second-chance points are locked in, which covers for a group that won't play fast.

bench.helps: Damon Wilkinson is a starter-grade big (81) coming off the bench — 13.9/6.4 on 58.9% shooting with 0.8 blocks, making him the team's best rim protector and rebounder despite backing up Kapke. Degourville (3.0 apg) is a legitimate backup point, and Jacobsen (36.6% from three, 1.0 stl) is a trustworthy 3-and-D guard.
bench.hurts: The guard/wing depth is thin and inefficient. Essegian cratered to 31.8% FG and 25.8% from three; freshmen Rice and Lanier are unproven; and backup PG Degourville simply can't score (37.1% FG, 34.5% 3P). A Leonhardt breather can turn into a scoring drought.

coach.might: Ride the two returning wings and the portal spine: Leonhardt on the ball, Sandfort as the clear first option, five-out spacing with Orme and Kapke stretching the floor, and Wilkinson as the first big off the bench.
should: Weaponize the five-out look — run Sandfort off pin-downs and flares, and put Orme (39.7%) and Kapke (33.3%) in pick-and-pop to drag the only interior defenders out of the paint and open Leonhardt's drives.

Solve the rim by minutes: no starter deters anything (Kapke 0.4 blk), so give Wilkinson (0.8 blk, 6-10, 58.9% FG) starter-level run as the defensive anchor — even start him over Kapke in physical B10 games and use Kapke as the stretch-five.
Never sit Leonhardt and Sandfort together. The roster has exactly one distributor and one creator with no replacement for either; stagger them so one is always on the floor to run the offense.

Manufacture the defense you can't get at the rim — lean into Leonhardt's ball pressure (2.1 stl) and gang rebounding, and trust Jacobsen (36.6% 3P, 1.0 stl) over Essegian (25.8% 3P) as the first guard off the bench.

Nebraska.essence: A mixed build that's smarter than a pure portal overhaul: the two best players — wings Pryce Sandfort (92) and Braden Frager (89) — are returners, and Hoiberg reconstructed the spine around them through the portal (Leonhardt/Utah Valley at the point, Orme/Belmont at the four, Kapke/Boston College at the five). The identity is five-out spacing and clean usage fit — one true alpha in Sandfort, a pass-first engine in Leonhardt, and efficient low-usage finishers around them. The flaws are just as clear: for all the 6-9-to-6-11 size, this lineup does not protect the rim, the playmaking begins and ends with Leonhardt, and several new pieces are jumping up multiple levels of competition.

second_unit.strength: The frontcourt. Wilkinson gives the second unit a better rim-protecting, rebounding anchor (0.8 blk, 6.4 rpg, 58.9% FG) than the starter he sits behind — the bench actually upgrades the interior defense the starting five lacks.
second_unit.weakness: Perimeter creation and shot-making. Degourville can't score, Essegian is a negative shooter (25.8% 3P), and there's no bench alpha, so the second unit only functions with Leonhardt or Sandfort staggered into it.

flaws.b: Kapke blocks 0.4 a game, Orme 0.7, Sandfort 0.3 — the whole starting five combines for roughly 1.7. There is real size on the roster and essentially zero rim protection in the lineup. B10 guards will get downhill and finish.
flaws.t: 6-11 and 6-9, and nobody blocks a shot

flaws.b: 6.0 apg from him, then a cliff: Sandfort 2.0, everyone else 1.8 or below. Pressure him (2.7 TOV already) or sit him and there is no secondary engine to run the offense.
flaws.t: Playmaking starts and ends with Leonhardt

flaws.b: Behind Sandfort, nobody manufactures a bucket. Frager scores 11.8 but on 1.0 apg — a catch-and-shoot piece, not a creator. When Sandfort rests, half-court offense gets hard in a hurry.
flaws.t: No secondary shot creator

flaws.b: Leonhardt (Utah Valley), Orme (Belmont), Wilkinson (South Dakota State) all put up numbers against mid-major competition. The B10 will test whether 13.9 and 12.7 a night actually travels.
flaws.t: Level-jump questions across the new spine

positives.b: All five starters shoot it. Sandfort (41.6%) and Orme (39.7%) are the genuine 39%+ pair, but Leonhardt (36.8%), Frager (35.2%) and even 6-11 Kapke (33.3%) all stretch the floor. There's no non-shooter clogging the lane, which is exactly what opens Leonhardt's driving game.
positives.t: True five-out — no one to ignore

positives.b: This is the opposite of a ball-hog collision. Sandfort is the lone high-volume scorer (18.1 ppg) and Leonhardt is a 6.0-apg facilitator; Orme (55.9% FG) and Kapke (47.9%) are efficient low-usage finishers. Nobody's touches step on anybody else's.
positives.t: Clean usage fit — one alpha, one distributor

positives.b: 18.1 ppg on 41.6% from three and 85.5% at the line with just 0.7 turnovers a game. A 92-grade returning wing who scores at volume without coughing it up is the cleanest foundation on the roster.
positives.t: Sandfort is a star, and absurdly efficient

positives.b: Leonhardt rebounds like a wing (5.4 rpg) and pressures the ball (2.1 stl) from the point, and the starters gang-rebound — Kapke 5.7, Orme 5.0, Sandfort 4.9 — to cover for the lack of one dominant board man.

bench.helps: Braeden Smith (79, from Gonzaga) is the best bench piece and arguably the answer to the roster's biggest hole — 3.6 apg in just 17 mpg with a 1.0 steal, a real pass-first lead guard who can stabilize the offense the freshman starter can't yet. Devin Brown (76, Davidson) gives a 6-6 wing with size, and Ahneman (6-11) plus Solongo (7-1) offer rim size to spell Duncomb.
bench.hurts: The quality cliff after Smith is steep — grades tumble to 74, 71, 71, 65 and down. Brown shot only 31% from three and 63% from the line, Imes 32.5%/52.4% from the line, Dortch scored 2.1 ppg — the bench shooters aren't shooters. Beyond Smith, this is bodies and size, not production, and the bigs (Ahneman, Solongo) are unproven with no college sample.

coach.might: Run everything through Duncomb in the post, start the freshman Sanderson at the point, and space the floor with Roberts and Braeden Shrewsberry — a big, efficient, inside-out starting five that leans on its 40% shooters and its 60% post scorer.
should: Stagger Braeden Smith's minutes to overlap the bench — never let a Sanderson-off lineup sit without a true creator; Smith's 3.6 apg is the safety valve for a freshman-led backcourt, so treat him as a starter-level rotation piece, not a reserve.

Weaponize Duncomb as a passing hub, not just a scorer — with two 40% shooters spotting up (Roberts, Shrewsberry) and a stretch-four in Koehler, post touches should trigger kick-outs; the spacing is elite around him even if the guards can't yet create off the bounce.

Protect the rim by committee and scheme, not personnel — with no shot-blocker (0.8 and 0.7 blocks up front), sit in a disciplined half-court shell, wall up drives, and be deliberate about not leaving the paint unmanned when Duncomb rests his 24.3 minutes.

Play Koehler as a genuine 6-10 floor-spacer at the four — his 38.2% from three is the lineup lever that lets you keep two bigs on the court without clogging Duncomb's post space; don't bury a stretch weapon that rare on the bench.

Notre Dame.essence: A returning-core-plus-targeted-portal build rather than a teardown — Shrewsberry keeps his son Braeden, Koehler, and Imes and bolts on two proven scorers in Logan Duncomb (18.3/8.9 from Winthrop) and Ethan Roberts (16.9 on 40.4% from Penn). The identity is size and efficient half-court scoring through a dominant post: Duncomb is a 60% interior hub, flanked by legitimate wing shooting. The tension is on the perimeter — a true freshman (Sanderson) is penciled in at the point, real lead-guard playmaking lives on the bench in Braeden Smith, and for all the 6-10/6-11/7-1 bodies there is no genuine rim protector. Good shooting, good size, a clear number-one option — but open questions at the game's two most important spots: who runs it and who guards the rim.

second_unit.strength: Ball movement and steadiness — Smith (3.6 apg) finally puts a true distributor on the floor, and pairing him with Brown's 6-6 size and a fresh big (Ahneman/Solongo) gives a defensible, size-first second unit that can control tempo and feed the post.
second_unit.weakness: It can't shoot or score. Take Smith's passing away and the bench is a collection of sub-33% shooters (Brown 31%, Imes 32.5%) and low-usage bigs; there's no bench bucket-getter, so any lineup without a starter scorer risks stalling in the half court.

flaws.b: Sanderson (Fr, 76, no college sample) is the penciled-in starting PG. On a team built to win now around two grad-transfer scorers, handing the keys to an unproven freshman is the single biggest bet on the roster — and there's no proven creation behind him in the starting five.
flaws.t: A freshman is running the offense

flaws.b: The starting five's assist leader is Roberts at 2.3, and he's a scorer, not a distributor. Duncomb (1.6), Shrewsberry (1.9) and Koehler (0.3) don't create for others. If Sanderson isn't ready, nobody in this group generates easy shots.
flaws.t: Playmaking is dangerously thin

flaws.b: Duncomb blocked 0.8, Koehler 0.7 — for a front line of 6-10s, that's soft. This team is big but not a shot-eraser; drivers who beat the first line will find the paint open, and Duncomb averaging 24.3 mpg means the rim is unguarded when he sits.
flaws.t: No rim protector despite all the size

flaws.b: Braeden Shrewsberry hit 40.2% from three but only 39% from the floor overall — he's a catch-and-shoot spacer, not a shot-creator (1.9 apg, 11.9 ppg). Valuable next to Duncomb, but he doesn't solve the who-creates-off-the-dribble problem.
flaws.t: Shrewsberry's shooting is spacing, not scoring

positives.b: Duncomb (89 grade) went 18.3/8.9 on 60% from the floor at Winthrop — a genuine interior hub who scores efficiently, draws help, and rebounds his position. Every set can start with a touch here, and at 6-10 he's a matchup problem inside.
positives.t: A true number-one option in the post

positives.b: Roberts (40.4% on volume, 16.9 ppg) and Braeden Shrewsberry (40.2%) are two legitimate 40% threats on the perimeter. Duncomb kick-outs have live targets — you cannot pack the paint against this starting group without paying for it from deep.
positives.t: Real wing shooting flanks the star

positives.b: 16.9/3.9/2.3 on 40% from three at Penn, 84 grade — a plug-and-play second scorer who can create a little (2.3 apg) and shoot a lot. He takes creation pressure off a freshman point guard.

Koehler (6-10) and Duncomb (6-10) start, and Koehler is a stretch four who hit 38.2% from three in limited run — a 6-10 floor-spacer is a real weapon. This group is big without going non-shooting at the four.
positives.t: Elite size across the front line
